segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then Pilate took Jesus and had him flogged.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the soldiers wove a crown out of thorns and put it on his head, and they wrapped a purple robe around him,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and they kept coming up to him, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Hail, King of the Jews!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and slapping him in the face.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Pilate went outside again and said to them,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Look, I am bringing him out to you, so that you may know that I find no grounds for a charge against him.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So Jesus came outside, wearing the crown of thorns and the purple robe. And Pilate said to them,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Here is the man!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When the chief priests and the officers saw him, they shouted,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Crucify! Crucify!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Pilate said to them,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Take him yourselves and crucify him, for I find no grounds for a charge against him.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The Jewish leaders answered him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “We have a law, and according to that law he ought to die, because he made himself Son of God.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When Pilate heard this statement, he became even more afraid,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and he went back into the governor’s headquarters and said to Jesus,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Where are you from?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Jesus gave him no answer.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So Pilate said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “You will not speak to me? Do you not know that I have authority to release you and authority to crucify you?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus answered him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “You would have no authority over me at all if it had not been given to you from above. For this reason the one who handed me over to you has the greater sin.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: From then on Pilate tried to release him, but the Jewish leaders shouted,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “If you release this man, you are no friend of Caesar. Everyone who makes himself king opposes Caesar.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So when Pilate heard these words, he brought Jesus outside and sat down on the judge’s seat at a place called the Stone Pavement, or in Hebrew, Gabbatha.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now it was the day of Preparation of the Passover, about the sixth hour. And he said to the Jewish leaders,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Here is your king!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They shouted,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Away with him! Away with him! Crucify him!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Pilate said to them,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Shall I crucify your king?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The chief priests answered,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “We have no king but Caesar.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he handed him over to them to be crucified. So they took charge of Jesus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And carrying the cross himself, he went out to what is called the Place of the Skull, which in Hebrew is called Golgotha,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: where they crucified him, and with him two others, one on either side, with Jesus in the middle.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Pilate also wrote a notice and put it on the cross. It read: “Jesus the Nazarene, the King of the Jews.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Many of the Jews read this notice, because the place where Jesus was crucified was near the city, and it was written in Hebrew, in Latin, and in Greek.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So the chief priests of the Jews said to Pilate,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Do not write ‘The King of the Jews,’ but that this man said, ‘I am King of the Jews.’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Pilate answered,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “What I have written, I have written.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When the soldiers had crucified Jesus, they took his clothes and divided them into four shares, a share for each soldier, and they took the tunic as well. Now the tunic was seamless, woven from the top in one piece throughout.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So they said to one another,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Let us not tear it, but cast lots for it, to see whose it will be.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: This was so that the scripture would be fulfilled that says,

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “They divided my clothes among themselves, and for my clothing they cast lots.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So that is what the soldiers did.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now standing by the cross of Jesus were his mother and his mother’s sister, Mary the wife of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When Jesus saw his mother, and the disciple whom he loved standing nearby, he said to his mother,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Woman, here is your son.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he said to the disciple,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Here is your mother.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And from that hour the disciple took her into his own home.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After this, knowing that everything was now finished, and so that the scripture would be completed, Jesus said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “I am thirsty.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: A jar full of sour wine was standing there. So they put a sponge full of the sour wine on a hyssop stalk and held it up to his mouth.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When Jesus had taken the sour wine, he said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “It is finished.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he bowed his head and handed over his spirit.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Since it was the day of Preparation, the Jewish leaders did not want the bodies to remain on the crosses during the Sabbath, for that Sabbath was a great day. So they asked Pilate to have their legs broken and the bodies taken away.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So the soldiers came and broke the legs of the first man, and then of the other who had been crucified with him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But when they came to Jesus and saw that he was already dead, they did not break his legs,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but one of the soldiers stabbed his side with a spear, and at once blood and water came out.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The one who saw it has testified, and his testimony is true, and he knows that he is telling the truth, so that you also may believe.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For these things happened so that the scripture would be fulfilled:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “Not a bone of his will be broken.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And again, another scripture says,

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “They will look on the one they pierced.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After this, Joseph of Arimathea, who was a disciple of Jesus, though a secret one for fear of the Jewish leaders, asked Pilate to let him take away the body of Jesus, and Pilate gave permission. So he came and took away his body.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Nicodemus also came, the one who had first come to him by night, bringing a mixture of myrrh and aloes weighing about a hundred pounds.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So they took the body of Jesus and bound it in linen cloths with the spices, as is the burial custom of the Jews.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now in the place where he was crucified there was a garden, and in the garden a new tomb in which no one had yet been laid.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So, because it was the day of Preparation of the Jews and the tomb was close by, they laid Jesus there.

notes.note: The Greek says simply 'the Jews', and most translations keep that. In this trial scene the group pressing Pilate is the Jerusalem authorities (the chief priests and their officers of verse 6), not the Jewish people as a whole, so the narrower rendering is used here and in verses 12, 14, 31 and 38. Scholars are divided on how to translate the word: some argue for 'Judeans' throughout, others object that this erases Jews from the New Testament.

'Friend of Caesar' was a recognised term for someone who enjoyed the emperor's favour, and losing that standing could end a career or worse. Whether Pilate held it as a formal title is uncertain. Either way, the threat is that releasing a self-declared king would be reported to Rome as disloyalty.

The Greek verb can also mean 'seated (someone)', so the sentence could say that Pilate seated Jesus on the judge's seat, as a mocking presentation of him as king. A minority of scholars read it that way. Most take it as Pilate himself sitting to give judgment, which is the usual sense of this verb form in the New Testament.

The Greek word means 'in the language of the Hebrews'. Gabbatha and Golgotha (verse 17) are Aramaic in form, and Greek writers of the period did not always distinguish Hebrew from Aramaic, the everyday language of many Jews in Palestine. For that reason many modern translations render 'in Aramaic' here.

notes.phrase: the day of Preparation of the Passover
notes.note: 'Preparation' was the ordinary name for Friday, the day on which preparations were made for the Sabbath. The phrase can therefore mean 'the Friday of Passover week' or 'the day of preparing for the Passover meal'. The choice bears on whether John dates the crucifixion to the day before Passover began, and the question is disputed.

Hours were counted from sunrise, so the sixth hour is about noon. Mark 15:25 places the crucifixion at the third hour, and the difference has long been discussed without an agreed solution. Some interpreters think John's timing is meant to recall the hour when the slaughter of the Passover lambs began.

notes.phrase: his mother and his mother’s sister, Mary the wife of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene
notes.traditional: his mother, and his mother's sister, Mary the wife of Cleophas, and Mary Magdalene
notes.note: The Greek can be read as naming four women, with the mother's sister unnamed, or three, with 'Mary of Clopas' being the sister. Most scholars count four, partly because two sisters both named Mary would be unusual. The Greek says only 'Mary of Clopas'; 'wife' is the most likely relationship, but daughter or mother is possible.

In Greek this was a normal and courteous way to address a woman, without the coldness the word carries in English. Jesus addresses other women the same way in this Gospel. It is nonetheless an unusual way for a son to address his mother, and interpreters differ on what it implies.

John uses his usual word for scripture being 'fulfilled' in verses 24 and 36. Here he uses a different verb, one that shares its root with 'finished' in this verse and in verse 30, and 'completed' keeps that echo. The clause could also attach to what precedes ('everything was now finished so that the scripture would be completed'), but most interpreters link it to Jesus's words 'I am thirsty'.

This was a cheap, sharp wine, usually diluted with water, the everyday drink of soldiers and labourers. Older English versions say 'vinegar', which suggests something undrinkable. It was in fact a common thirst-quencher, and the jar most likely belonged to the soldiers.

The verb is the same one used in this chapter for Jesus being 'handed over' to Pilate and to crucifixion (verses 11 and 16), and the rendering keeps that repetition. It presents Jesus's death as his own deliberate act. Some interpreters also see a hint of the giving of the Spirit, since the Greek says literally 'the spirit', but most take the phrase simply as a description of his death.

The Greek says 'that one knows', and it is not certain who 'that one' is. Most take it as the eyewitness himself, usually identified with the disciple whom Jesus loved. Others think the writer is appealing to a second party, either the witness as distinct from the writer, or Christ or God as guarantor of the testimony.

notes.phrase: “Not a bone of his will be broken.”
notes.traditional: A bone of him shall not be broken
notes.note: The wording is closest to the rule for the Passover lamb, whose bones were not to be broken (Exodus 12:46; Numbers 9:12). It also resembles Psalm 34:20, about God guarding the bones of the righteous. Many scholars think John has both in view, presenting Jesus as the Passover lamb and as the righteous sufferer.
The unit is the Roman pound, about 327 grams, so the total is roughly 33 kilograms, or about 72 modern pounds. This is a very large and costly quantity of spices, on the scale of a royal burial.

candidates.reason: It runs through all the passion narratives and Paul with renderings varying between 'betray', 'deliver', 'hand over' and 'give up', which hides a deliberate thread.
Translations split between the loanword 'Praetorium', 'palace', 'headquarters' and 'judgment hall' across the Gospels, Acts and Philippians.
Translations vary between 'in Hebrew' and 'in Aramaic' in John, Acts and Revelation, and one policy is needed.
It occurs across the Gospels and Acts and is rendered either 'of Nazareth' or 'the Nazarene/Nazorean', and the relation to Ναζαρηνός needs a single decision.
It occurs in all four passion narratives, where the choice between 'Preparation', 'day of Preparation' and 'Friday' affects how readers understand the chronology.
